title: T/F/NI + Vocabulary: The Repair Cafe Movement (poziom rejonowy/wojewodzki)

tasks.instruction: Przeczytaj ponizszy tekst. Zdecyduj, ktore zdania (1.1.–1.6.) sa zgodne z trescia tekstu (T – True), ktore sa niezgodne (F – False), a ktore zawieraja informacje niepodane w tekscie (NI – No Information). Nastepnie znajdz w tekscie wyrazy lub wyrazenia, ktore odpowiadaja definicjom podanym w punktach 1.7.–1.11. Wymagana jest calkowita poprawnosc ortograficzna odpowiedzi.
tasks.text:
BRING US YOUR BROKEN THINGS

On the second Saturday of every month, the community hall on my street fills up with toasters. Also lamps, bicycles, jumpers with holes in the elbow, a sewing machine that has not worked since 1988, and once, memorably, an accordion. The people who bring them are not dropping them off. They are staying, and that distinction is the whole point.

The first repair cafe opened in Amsterdam in October 2009. It was the idea of Martine Postma, a journalist who had been writing about waste and had grown tired of writing about waste. Her plan was simple enough to explain in a sentence: put people who know how to mend things in a room with people who own broken things, add coffee, and see what happens. About fifty people came to that first session. There are now well over two thousand repair cafes in more than thirty countries, and the foundation Postma set up sends out a starter pack to anybody who wants to open one.

What the starter pack insists on is the rule I mentioned. You do not hand your kettle to the volunteer and come back in an hour. You sit down next to them, you hold the torch, and you are shown what is being done and why. Postma has always argued that the mending is only half of it. The objects, she says, are a way of getting at something larger: a generation that has never seen the inside of an appliance and has no reason to believe that the inside is anything other than a mystery. Once you have watched somebody replace a two-pound switch in a kettle you were about to throw away, the next broken thing looks different.

This is less straightforward than it was. Anyone who has tried to open a modern appliance knows how daunting the first five minutes can be: cases glued rather than screwed, screws with heads shaped so that no ordinary screwdriver will fit, batteries sealed in place, and diagnostic software that refuses to talk to a part it does not recognise. Some of this is genuinely about making things thinner and more waterproof. Some of it is planned obsolescence, and manufacturers have on the whole made repair harder over the past fifteen years rather than easier. Repair cafes have become an unlikely lobbying force in response, and volunteers keep records of what comes in and what defeats them; those records have found their way into the arguments for right-to-repair legislation in Europe.

Not everything gets fixed. The honest figure, across the movement, is that a bit under two-thirds of items leave working. What surprises new volunteers is how little the failures matter to the people who brought the items in. A man at our hall spent forty minutes with a volunteer on a radio that had belonged to his father, established that the fault was in a component nobody has made since the 1970s, and went home visibly happier than he had arrived, because now he knew.

Our cafe has never advertised. It grew entirely by word of mouth, which appears to be the norm. It also has a waiting list of volunteers, which nobody expected; it turns out that a retired electrician with an afternoon free is a considerable natural resource.

None of this is going to solve anything on its own. Britain throws away well over a million tonnes of electrical goods a year, and the throwaway habit shows no sign of being on the wane. Two thousand church halls will not turn that around. But every month a few hundred thousand people somewhere in the world sit down beside a stranger, take the back off something, and discover that it was never a mystery in the first place. Postma's argument was always that this is the part that lasts, long after the toaster has finally died.

items.statement: The text names the person who started the first repair cafe.
items.explanation: TRUE — 'It was the idea of Martine Postma, a journalist who had been writing about waste'.

items.statement: Visitors to a repair cafe leave their broken items with a volunteer and collect them later.
items.explanation: FALSE — 'You do not hand your kettle to the volunteer and come back in an hour. You sit down next to them, you hold the torch'.

items.statement: Repair cafes in Britain receive money from the national government.
items.explanation: NO INFORMATION — The text mentions right-to-repair legislation and a starter pack from Postma's foundation, but says nothing about government funding.

items.statement: Postma's purpose went beyond getting individual objects working again.
items.explanation: TRUE — 'the mending is only half of it. The objects, she says, are a way of getting at something larger'.

items.statement: According to the text, manufacturers have made their products easier to repair in recent years.
items.explanation: FALSE — 'manufacturers have on the whole made repair harder over the past fifteen years rather than easier'.

items.statement: Items brought to repair cafes are more likely to be mended successfully if they are electrical.
items.explanation: NO INFORMATION — The text gives one overall success rate of 'a bit under two-thirds' but never breaks it down by type of item.

vocabItems.definition: making you feel nervous or worried because something seems difficult
the practice of designing products so that they stop being useful after a certain time
information passed from one person to another in conversation rather than through advertising
becoming gradually smaller, weaker or less important
generally, when everything is taken into account
